lead: CPU scheduling decides which ready process gets the CPU next. Different policies trade off simplicity, response time, and fairness. The classic algorithms – First‑Come‑First‑Served, Shortest‑Job‑First, priority, and Round‑Robin – appear in most Indian B.Tech syllabi. They are used in desktop OSes, in transaction servers handling UPI payments, and in embedded controllers of railway ticket kiosks.
prereq: You need the concepts of process states and context switching from process scheduling queues and context switching.

blocks.text: FCFS puts processes in the ready queue in order of arrival. The scheduler never changes this order. It is easy to implement but can give large waiting time if a long process arrives before short ones.

items: When a process arrives, append it to the tail of the ready queue.
When the CPU becomes idle, remove the head of the queue and dispatch it.

blocks.text: SJF is non‑preemptive. At each dispatch the scheduler looks at all processes that have arrived and selects the one with the smallest CPU burst. This reduces average waiting time but needs knowledge of burst length.

items: Advantage: minimum average waiting time among non‑preemptive policies.
Requires either past statistics or programmer hints.

blocks.where: WT_i is waiting time of process i; n is number of processes.

blocks.text: Each process is assigned a priority number. Lower numbers mean higher priority in most Indian curricula. The scheduler always picks the ready process with the highest priority (lowest number).

items: When a process arrives, insert it into the ready queue sorted by priority.
If two processes have the same priority, break the tie by FCFS order.
Preemptive version can interrupt a running low‑priority process when a higher‑priority one arrives.

blocks.text: In many real‑time systems priority scheduling is combined with aging – gradually increasing the priority of waiting jobs – to avoid starvation.
RR gives each process a fixed CPU slice called a quantum. After the quantum expires, the process is placed at the tail of the ready queue and the next process runs.

items: Select the head of the ready queue.
Run it for at most quantum ms.
If the process finishes earlier, remove it; otherwise, enqueue the remaining part at the tail.
Advantage: good average response time, suitable for time‑sharing systems.
Disadvantage: too small a quantum causes many context switches; too large degrades to FCFS.
Quantum is often chosen as 20‑40 ms in desktop OSes.

blocks.text: RR is the default scheduler for many interactive services such as IRCTC ticket booking where many short requests share the CPU.

examples.question: Three processes arrive as follows: P1 at 0 ms with burst 8 ms; P2 at 1 ms with burst 4 ms; P3 at 2 ms with burst 2 ms and priority 1 (high). Using a quantum of 4 ms for Round‑Robin, draw the Gantt chart for FCFS, SJF (non‑preemptive), Priority (non‑preemptive) and RR. Compute the average waiting time for each algorithm.
steps: FCFS order is P1 → P2 → P3 because the queue follows arrival time.
SJF picks the shortest ready burst at each dispatch. At t=0 only P1 is ready, so run P1[0‑8]. At t=8, P2 and P3 are ready; choose P3 (burst 2) then P2 (burst 4).
Priority uses the given priority numbers (lower = higher). At t=0 only P1, so run P1[0‑8]. At t=8, P2 and P3 are ready; P3 has higher priority, so same order as SJF.
Priority Gantt and waiting times are identical to SJF, giving average waiting 5 ms.
Round‑Robin with quantum 4 ms: first slice P1[0‑4], then P2[4‑8] (P2 finishes), then P3[8‑10] (P3 finishes), then remaining P1[10‑14].
Waiting times: WT(P1)= (10‑4) =6 ms, WT(P2)=4‑1=3 ms, WT(P3)=8‑2=6 ms.
examples.answer: Average waiting times: FCFS 5.67 ms, SJF 5 ms, Priority 5 ms, Round‑Robin 5 ms.
examples.check:
import math
# data
arrival = {'P1':0,'P2':1,'P3':2}
burst = {'P1':8,'P2':4,'P3':2}
# FCFS
wt_fcfs = [0, 8-1, 12-2]
avg_fcfs = sum(wt_fcfs)/3
# SJF (non‑preemptive)
wt_sjf = [0, 10-1, 8-2]
avg_sjf = sum(wt_sjf)/3
# Priority (same as SJF here)
wt_pri = wt_sjf
avg_pri = avg_sjf
# RR quantum 4
wt_rr = [6, 4-1, 8-2]
avg_rr = sum(wt_rr)/3
for v in [avg_fcfs, avg_sjf, avg_pri, avg_rr]:
    print(round(v,2))

traps: Ignoring arrival times and ordering FCFS simply by process number.
Treating SJF as preemptive; the non‑preemptive version does not interrupt a running job.
Using priority number as “higher is larger” when the syllabus defines lower numbers as higher priority.
Choosing a quantum that is larger than any burst, which makes RR identical to FCFS and defeats the purpose.
For average waiting time, forgetting to subtract the arrival time from the start time of each process.

quiz.q: Why can SJF produce the minimum average waiting time among non‑preemptive algorithms?
quiz.a: Because it always executes the shortest CPU burst first, reducing the time later processes wait.

quiz.q: Given processes A( arrival 0, burst 5 ), B( arrival 2, burst 3 ), C( arrival 4, burst 1 ), compute the average waiting time using non‑preemptive SJF.
quiz.a: Order: A[0‑5], C[5‑6], B[6‑9]. Waiting times: A 0, C 1, B 4. Avg = (0+1+4)/3 = 1.67 ms.

quiz.q: In Round‑Robin with quantum 3 ms, a process with burst 7 ms will run how many times and for how long each time?
quiz.a: It will run three times: first two slices of 3 ms each, then a final slice of 1 ms.

quiz.q: If a system uses only priority scheduling without aging, what problem can appear and how does aging solve it?
quiz.a: Low‑priority processes may starve because higher‑priority jobs keep arriving. Aging gradually increases the priority of waiting jobs, eventually allowing them to run.

quiz.q: What is the main parameter that decides the behavior of Round‑Robin?
Explain why a very small quantum can degrade system performance.
quiz.a: A tiny quantum causes many context switches, increasing overhead and reducing the time spent doing useful work.

quiz.q: A process arrives at 0 ms with burst 10 ms. Another arrives at 5 ms with burst 2 ms. Under preemptive SJF, when does the second process start?
quiz.a: At 5 ms, because the newly arrived process has a shorter total burst (2 ms) than the remaining burst (5 ms) of the first process, so it preempts and starts at 5 ms.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern operating systems blend these classic policies with dynamic load monitoring, using multi‑level feedback queues to adapt quantum size and priority. Real‑time kernels add deadline‑based schedulers such as EDF (Earliest Deadline First). Research on energy‑aware scheduling integrates DVFS (dynamic voltage and frequency scaling) to reduce power while meeting performance goals. To explore further, search for "multilevel feedback queue" and "real‑time deadline scheduling" in recent OS conference papers.
